newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu heads to Jordan for talks with king.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu heads to Jordan for talks with king.

text.p: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu travelled to Jordan on Wednesday for talks with King Hussein, who was expected to press him to ease sanctions on Palestinians.
Netanyahu, who imposed the punitive measures after suicide bombers killed 14 people in Jerusalem last month, was unlikely to comply.

"We have a very positive approach to some of the suggestions made by King Hussein," Israeli government spokesman Moshe Fogel said after Jordan's foreign minister said Amman would urge Israel to lift a two-week blockade of the West Bank and Gaza.
"But I can tell you as far as we're concerned it's crucial to have the Palestinian Authority take concrete actions against terror and they haven't done it yet," he told Reuters.
The Jordan summit in the Red Sea resort of Aqaba comes after Washington on Tuesday described a mission by a U.S. envoy to restore security cooperation between Israel and the PLO as encouraging.

U.S. mediator Dennis Ross has shuttled between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat since Sunday, managing to bring Israeli and Palestinian security officials together for intelligence sharing.
Israel says the meetings must be accompanied by a PLO crackdown on Islamic militants who have killed scores of Israelis in suicide bombings since 1994.

"We want and are interested in cancelling those measures which won't be necessary when -- we hope -- the Palestinian Authority fulfils its commitments," said Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, who was accompanying Netanyahu to Jordan.
But the Palestinian side links security cooperation with political progress in peacemaking and demands a halt to Israeli settlement building in the West Bank.

"This has been a good start and the process has been set in motion. We have to see the process produce results and we're working to that end," Ross told reporters after meeting Arafat in the West Bank town of Ramallah.
In Washington, a State Department spokesman said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was encouraged by the results of Ross's mission.

During their talks with Ross, the two sides determined a means of sharing information and acting together to combat terrorism, spokesman James Rubin said, adding: "Now we're going to be looking for results, results, results."
Ross was expected to meet again with Arafat and Netanyahu on Wednesday before heading home to prepare a possible first visit to the region by Albright later this month.

Palestinian negotiator Nabil Shaath said Ross had extended his visit to Wednesday in order to persuade Israel to lift the closure imposed on the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the bomb attack on July 30 and to rescind other measures.

"I think Mr Ross is doing his best to get started and this means getting the tripartite security coordinations started and it also means for Israel to rescind all the measures it has taken against us," he told reporters in Ramallah.
Israel-PLO peacemaking has been dormant since March when Netanyahu's government allowed construction to begin of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
The twin suicide bombing plunged their already precarious ties deeper into crisis, with Netanyahu accusing Arafat of tacitly condoning militants who oppose the Israel-PLO peace moves.
Arafat has insisted he is making a "100 percent effort" on security and accuses Israel of using the bombing as a pretext to weaken his legitimacy.
In Damascus, President Hafez al-Assad renewed his commitment to making peace with Israel, saying Syria did not wish to go to war with the Jewish state.

"We want peace and if we did not there could not have been a peace process," presidential spokesman Joubran Kourieh quoted Assad as telling 44 visiting Israeli Arab delegates, including members of parliament and opposition Labour and Meretz parties.
Assad also said Damascus would not accept a peace that did not return the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in 1967, to Syria and accused Netanyahu of blocking the peace process.
Peace talks between Syria and Israel have been suspended for nearly 18 months.
